claims.text: A defect-informed predictive model will predict the thermal and electronic conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The proposed accuracy advantage applies across the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The modeled bulk HfNbTaTiZr contains an intentionally controlled oxygen impurity concentration of 1 wt.%.
The proposed computational approach combines ab initio defect energetics with transport simulations and explicitly represents structural defects and impurity scattering.
Quantum effects and impurity scattering dominate conductivity behavior in the nearly 0–200 K regime.
Enhanced phonon contributions and defect interactions are significant in the 300–1200 K regime.
Oxygen impurities and other point defects alter local bonding relative to an ideal defect-free HfNbTaTiZr crystal.
Oxygen impurities and other point defects alter the electronic structure relative to an ideal defect-free HfNbTaTiZr crystal.
Defects modify the electronic band structure of HfNbTaTiZr.
Defects modify phonon-scattering mechanisms in HfNbTaTiZr.
At low temperatures, impurity scattering is a primary source of deviations in conductivity.
At high temperatures, defect–phonon interactions dominate the defect-related conductivity response.
Representing temperature-dependent defect effects will reduce prediction discrepancies to within experimental uncertainty in both temperature regimes.
Defect-induced localization and scattering effects are most pronounced in the low-temperature regime.
Phonon–defect scattering is significant in the high-temperature regime.
Existing analytical conductivity predictions typically assume perfect crystals and omit defects and impurities.
Omitting defects and impurities causes systematic discrepancies between existing analytical predictions and experiments when defect effects are non-negligible.
The approach is expected to apply to HfNbTaTiZr containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Above 1200 K or at substantially higher defect concentrations, other mechanisms may dominate and model accuracy may degrade.
Failure to improve prediction error over the perfect-crystal comparator, or failure of measurements to fall within predicted uncertainty bands in both regimes, would falsify the hypothesis.
